journeys.name: Polybius: hostage, companion and eyewitness
journeys.summary: The son of the Achaean general Lycortas, Polybius was one of the thousand leading Achaeans deported to Italy after Pydna on the say-so of the pro-Roman Callicrates. Where the others were parked in Etruscan towns, he was allowed to stay in Rome, where he became the mentor of the young Scipio Aemilianus. Seventeen years of detention turned him into the best-informed foreigner in Rome. Released in 150, he went where the history was being made: to Masinissa's court, to the siege of Carthage, along the Atlantic coast of Africa in a squadron lent by Scipio, to the ruins of Corinth, to Ptolemaic Alexandria and probably to Numantia. He also walked Hannibal's Alpine route to check the sources. The result was the Histories, written to explain how the Romans had conquered almost the whole inhabited world in less than 53 years (220-167).

journeys.name: Hannibal in exile, 195-183 BC
journeys.summary: After Zama Hannibal remained the most dangerous man in Carthage. As sufete in 196 he broke the grip of the judges' oligarchy and reformed the state finances so well that the indemnity could be paid without new taxes. His enemies told Rome he was plotting with Antiochus III, and when a Roman embassy arrived in 195 he rode through the night to his coastal estate, sailed for the Kerkennah islands and then for Tyre, the mother city. For twelve years he was a professional exile at Hellenistic courts: adviser to Antiochus, admiral of a Seleucid fleet beaten off Side, a fugitive on Crete, perhaps the planner of Artaxata for the Armenian king, finally a guest of Prusias of Bithynia. When Flamininus demanded his surrender he took poison at Libyssa.

journeys.name: Cicero in exile, 58-57 BC
journeys.summary: Clodius' bill outlawing anyone who had executed a citizen without trial was aimed at the consul of 63, and Cicero left Rome before it passed rather than fight in the streets. A second law named him, set a radius of 400 (later 500) miles, and his house on the Palatine was torn down for a shrine of Libertas. His letters from exile are the most raw he wrote: he begged Atticus to explain why he had not killed himself and considered suicide on the voyage. He hid first in the south, refused by the governor of Sicily, then crossed to Greece and lodged with the quaestor Plancius at Thessalonica. When the tide in Rome turned, the centuriate assembly recalled him on 4 August 57. He landed at Brundisium on the 5th, his daughter's birthday, and walked into a Rome that met him at the gate.

journeys.name: Cicero governs Cilicia, 51-50 BC
journeys.summary: Pompey's law of 52 forced ex-consuls who had never governed a province into the job, and Cicero drew Cilicia, a sprawling command from Pamphylia to the Taurus with Cyprus attached and a Parthian invasion threatening Syria next door. He hated every day of it and counted them in his letters, yet he was an honest governor by Roman standards: he capped interest at 12 per cent, refused the customary gifts, and fought Brutus' agents who were squeezing Salamis on Cyprus at 48 per cent. With two weak legions he marched to the Cilician Gates, then turned on the mountain tribes of the Amanus, besieged Pindenissum for 57 days and was hailed imperator. He spent the next year asking for a triumph and arrived outside Rome just as the civil war began, his lictors still wreathed in laurel.

journeys.name: Pompey's flight after Pharsalus, 48 BC
journeys.summary: On the afternoon of 9 August 48 Pompey watched his cavalry break and rode back to his camp, then out of the back gate before Caesar's men stormed it. With a handful of friends he fled through the Vale of Tempe to the sea, slept in a fisherman's hut and got aboard a grain freighter. He picked up his wife Cornelia and his son Sextus at Mytilene, called at Attalia and Cyprus, and debated where to go: Parthia, Numidia or Egypt, whose boy king Ptolemy XIII owed his throne to Pompey's support for his father. Egypt won. On 28 September, the day before his 58th birthday, he was rowed ashore at Pelusium in a small boat and stabbed by Achillas and Septimius, a Roman who had served under him. Cornelia watched from the ship.

journeys.name: Cleopatra in Rome, 46-44 BC
journeys.summary: After the Alexandrian War Cleopatra came to Rome, probably in summer 46 for Caesar's quadruple triumph, in which her sister Arsinoe was paraded in chains. She stayed in Caesar's gardens across the Tiber with her brother-husband Ptolemy XIV and the infant Caesarion, and received the great men of Rome; Cicero, who disliked her intensely, called on her and later wrote 'I hate the queen'. Caesar set a gilded statue of her beside Venus Genetrix in his new forum, a provocation remembered for centuries. Whether she stayed two years or went home and returned in 45 is disputed. She was still in the city on the Ides of March and left in mid April 44, soon after which Ptolemy XIV died, leaving Caesarion as her co-ruler.

journeys.name: Augustus' eastern tour, 22-19 BC
journeys.summary: In autumn 22, after refusing the dictatorship during a famine, Augustus left Rome for three years. The tour was a working inspection of the provinces and a diplomatic offensive. In Sicily he founded colonies; in Greece he punished Athens and rewarded Sparta; he wintered twice on Samos, where an embassy from an Indian king arrived with a tiger and a man without arms. The central business was Parthia. With Tiberius leading an army into Armenia and Augustus himself in Syria, Phraates IV handed back the standards lost by Crassus at Carrhae and by Antony, without a battle. Augustus made it the signature achievement of the reign: coins with a kneeling Parthian, the Prima Porta breastplate, a triumphal arch in the Forum. On the way home he met Virgil in Athens; the poet died at Brundisium.

journeys.name: Ovid's journey into exile, AD 8-9
journeys.summary: In autumn AD 8 the most fashionable poet in Rome was summoned to Augustus and sent to the edge of the world: relegatio, not exile, so he kept his property and citizenship, but he had to live at Tomis on the Black Sea. The reasons were 'a poem and an error' (carmen et error): the Art of Love, and something he had seen that he never named, very likely connected with the scandal of the younger Julia. He left Rome on a December night, crossed the Adriatic in winter gales that he turned into poems, transferred ships at Corinth, and from Samothrace walked across Thrace while his ship went on through the straits. At Tomis he learned Getic, wrote the Tristia and the Letters from Pontus, and watched the Danube freeze. Neither Augustus nor Tiberius relented. He died there in 17 or 18.

journeys.name: Germanicus in the East, AD 17-19
journeys.summary: After his German triumph Germanicus received an extraordinary command over all the eastern provinces, with the stubborn Cn. Calpurnius Piso sent to govern Syria at the same time. His journey was half tour of the classical world, half state business, and it ended in one of the great scandals of Tiberius' reign. He visited Actium, where his two grandfathers had fought on opposite sides, entered Athens with a single lictor, consulted the oracle of Clarian Apollo, crowned a new king of Armenia at Artaxata, and annexed Cappadocia and Commagene. In early 19 he went to Egypt without permission, which no senator was allowed to enter, sailed up the Nile to the colossi of Memnon and Syene, and opened the granaries at Alexandria. Back in Syria he fell ill and died at Antioch on 10 October, convinced Piso and Plancina had poisoned him.

journeys.name: Paul's first missionary journey
journeys.summary: Sent out by the church at Antioch with Barnabas and the young John Mark, Paul began, according to Acts, in Barnabas' home island of Cyprus, where the proconsul Sergius Paullus listened to them at Paphos; a family of Sergii Paulli with estates near Pisidian Antioch is known from inscriptions, which may explain why they went there next. Mark went home from Perge, a split that later broke up the partnership. In the Roman colony of Pisidian Antioch Paul preached in the synagogue and turned to the gentiles when the synagogue turned against him, the pattern of the whole mission. At Lystra the crowd took Barnabas for Zeus and Paul for Hermes, then stoned Paul and left him for dead. They walked back over the same road to strengthen the new communities and sailed home from Attalia.

journeys.name: Paul's second missionary journey
journeys.summary: After the Jerusalem meeting settled that gentile converts need not be circumcised, Paul set out again, now with Silas, having quarrelled with Barnabas. He revisited the Galatian churches, took on Timothy at Lystra, and tried to go into Asia and Bithynia before a vision at Troas called him across to Macedonia: the moment Christianity reached Europe, and where the 'we' passages of Acts begin. At the Roman colony of Philippi he was beaten with rods and jailed until he announced that he was a citizen. Thessalonica and Beroea followed, then Athens, where he debated with Epicureans and Stoics on the Areopagus with little success. Corinth was the triumph: eighteen months, a large church, and a hearing before the proconsul Gallio, Seneca's brother, who threw the case out. That hearing is the fixed point of all Pauline chronology.

journeys.name: Paul's third missionary journey
journeys.summary: The third journey was centred on Ephesus, the capital of Asia, where Paul stayed between two and three years and from where most of the Corinthian correspondence was written. Acts ends the stay with a riot in the great theatre led by Demetrius the silversmith, whose trade in shrines of Artemis was suffering, the crowd chanting 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians' for two hours until the town clerk dispersed them. Paul then toured Macedonia and Greece, writing Romans in Corinth, and organised a collection of money from his gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem. To avoid a plot he went back overland through Macedonia, sailed down the coast of Asia, said a tearful farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus and reached Jerusalem for Pentecost, where he was arrested in the Temple.

journeys.name: Paul's voyage to Rome and the shipwreck on Malta
journeys.summary: After two years in custody at Caesarea Paul used his right as a citizen to appeal to Caesar, and the new procurator Festus sent him to Rome under a centurion named Julius. Acts 27 is the most detailed account of a sea voyage to survive from antiquity, full of sailors' practice: changing ships at Myra to an Alexandrian grain freighter, running in the lee of Crete, arguing about wintering at Fair Havens, being caught by the north-easter called Euraquilo, undergirding the hull with cables, throwing the cargo and tackle overboard, sounding twenty then fifteen fathoms in the dark. After fourteen days the 276 on board ran aground on Malta and all reached land. Three months later another Alexandrian ship, the Dioscuri, took them via Syracuse and Rhegium to Puteoli, and Christians walked out from Rome to meet Paul at Forum Appii.

journeys.name: Peter the Apostle: the traditional route
journeys.summary: Peter's movements are known from Acts and Paul's letters up to about 49; after that the record becomes tradition. In Acts he leads the Jerusalem community, travels to Samaria, Lydda and Joppa, and baptises the centurion Cornelius at Caesarea, the first gentile convert in the narrative. Arrested by Herod Agrippa I around 43-44, he escaped and 'went to another place'. Paul met him in Jerusalem and confronted him at Antioch over eating with gentiles (Galatians 2). A 'Cephas party' at Corinth suggests a visit there. That he came to Rome and was executed under Nero is reported by 1 Clement (c. 96), hinted at by Ignatius, and stated outright from the late 2nd century; the 'trophy' on the Vatican mentioned by the presbyter Gaius around 200 has been identified with the aedicula found beneath St Peter's in the 1940s.

journeys.name: Nero's tour of Greece, AD 66-67
journeys.summary: Nero had wanted to perform in Greece for years, and in September 66 he went, with Poppaea's successor Statilia Messalina, a claque of 5,000 trained applauders and Vespasian, who disgraced himself by falling asleep during a recital. The Greek festivals were rescheduled so that the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean games, normally spread over four years, fell in one season, and a musical contest was added at Olympia for the first time. Nero won 1,808 prizes, including the chariot race at Olympia, where he fell out of a ten-horse chariot and was crowned anyway. At the Isthmus he dug the first basket of earth for a canal and on 28 November 67 proclaimed the freedom of Achaea, exempting it from tribute. Meanwhile his freedman Helius warned him that Rome was close to revolt.

journeys.name: Hadrian's first great tour, 121-125
journeys.summary: Hadrian spent more than half his reign away from Rome, and the coin series commemorating his visits to the provinces (adventus, restitutor, exercitus types) are a map of a new idea of empire: not Rome and its conquests, but a commonwealth of provinces seen by its ruler. The first tour began with the armies. He inspected the Rhine legions, tightened discipline, slept in the open and ate camp food, and ordered a continuous palisade along the German frontier. In Britain he ordered the Wall 'to separate Romans from barbarians'. He wintered at Tarraco, where a slave attacked him with a sword. A Parthian crisis took him east in 123; he settled it by meeting the king in person. He then toured Asia Minor, where he probably met the Bithynian youth Antinous, was initiated at Eleusis, and returned to Rome via Sicily, climbing Etna to watch the sunrise.

journeys.name: Hadrian's second great tour, 128-132
journeys.summary: The second tour opened with a quick visit to Africa, where Hadrian watched the exercises of legio III Augusta at Lambaesis and delivered the speech whose fragments survive on the parade-ground monument, judging each manoeuvre like a drill-sergeant. Then he went east for six years. He wintered at Athens, toured Asia Minor and Syria, gave Palmyra the name Hadriana, wintered at Gerasa, where an arch still marks his visit, and refounded Jerusalem as the colony Aelia Capitolina, a decision that helped provoke the Bar Kokhba revolt. In Egypt he restored Pompey's tomb at Pelusium, debated with the scholars of the Museum, and hunted a lion in the Libyan desert. In October 130 Antinous drowned in the Nile; Hadrian founded Antinoopolis on the spot and filled the empire with statues of him. He dedicated the Olympieion at Athens in 131/132.

journeys.name: Marcus Aurelius on the northern front, 168-180
journeys.summary: The philosopher emperor spent most of his last twelve years in army camps on the Danube, fighting a war he had not chosen while plague emptied the cities. The Marcomanni and Quadi had broken through to Aquileia in 170, the first invasion of Italy in nearly three centuries. Marcus auctioned palace treasures to pay for the war, recruited slaves and gladiators, and campaigned from bases at Carnuntum and Sirmium. Book 1 of the Meditations was written 'among the Quadi, on the Granua', book 2 'at Carnuntum'. The revolt of Avidius Cassius in 175 took him east, where his wife Faustina died at Halala; he was initiated at Eleusis on the way home. In 178 he returned north, apparently planning new provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia, and died in March 180, at Vindobona according to Aurelius Victor, at Sirmium according to Tertullian.

journeys.name: Septimius Severus' last expedition to Britain, 208-211
journeys.summary: At 63 and crippled by gout, Severus took the whole court to Britain: his wife Julia Domna, both quarrelling sons, the praetorian prefect Papinian and the imperial treasury. The pretext was trouble from the Maeatae and Caledonians; Herodian thought the real aim was to get Caracalla and Geta out of Rome and away from its pleasures. York became for three years the capital of the empire. Severus was carried in a litter across the Forth, rebuilt the fortress at Carpow on the Tay, and lost men by the thousand in bogs and ambushes without ever forcing a battle. The Caledonians submitted in 209 and rose again in 210. Severus ordered his soldiers to kill everyone, then died at York on 4 February 211, advising his sons to 'agree with each other, enrich the soldiers and despise everyone else'.
